name: Jamal Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political groups, and we don’t sell anything. What you say is confidential; I’d like to hear what you’d say publicly and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. I’m Jamal Okafor, twenty-seven, and I lead a small carpentry crew on building sites. I rent a flat with my partner Nia; we’re not married and don’t have children.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day, including what you enjoy and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m usually at the site gate before seven, checking the drawings and handing out the first jobs. I’m best when a wall is out of square and the crew can fix it without wasting a sheet of board. The lifting and noise get to my back by late afternoon, and one missed week means trouble because we have less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the drawing app can catch a missing measurement, but it still can’t tell you why the old brickwork bows. My crew would use it if it saved a trip to the van, and then get on with the build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means a few less minutes on paperwork, not a new life. I still worry about a quiet month because there are few building jobs nearby and our savings are thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and use the site app to check measurements before we cut. This winter I’d put a small amount from each pay into the account Nia and I use for emergencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, because the change is small. The thin savings still sit in the back of my mind when I look at the rent date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the day would the app help with, and what would you still check yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use it to flag a mismatch between the plan and the materials list before the delivery turns up. I’d still put a tape on the opening myself, because a wrong cut costs us time and nobody else carries that board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If work went quiet for a month, what would you and Nia change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d pause takeaway meals and keep the rent and bus fares paid first. Nia’s wages cover some bills, but we’d both notice the missing site pay straight away.

say: The drawing app can catch a **missing measurement**, but it cannot explain every crooked wall.
We would use a tool that saves a **trip to the van** and then carry on.
think: A few minutes off the paperwork will not change my **day on site** much.
A quiet month still worries me because our **savings are thin** and nearby work is scarce.
do: Keep leading the carpentry crew and check measurements with the **site app**.
Set aside a small amount from each **pay** for the ****emergency account****.
feel: I feel **mostly steady**, with the rent date still on my mind.
S0.quote: I still worry about a quiet month because there are few building jobs nearby and our savings are thin.
fieldNote: Jamal speaks from his **site experience**, separating a useful check from skilled judgment.
His easy tone sits beside a real **income worry** tied to scarce local jobs.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew through its regular site work
Use the site app to flag drawing and material list mismatches
Move a small amount from each pay into the shared emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office will order materials quicker and send cleaner drawings to site. On our end I’d still need a good carpenter to make the pieces meet when the building is not square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the office needing fewer people to check orders, though faster planning does not tell me how many sites will open. My hands-on work is harder to copy today, but I do not know how long that advantage lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the estimating and drawing tools our contractor adopts, while keeping my crew’s carpentry work sharp. In the first year I’d ask the site manager for a chance to price small jobs, and keep saving from each pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about fewer starts and an uncertain future for site work. I feel I can learn the new estimating system, but my small savings don’t give me much room to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to learn to price a small job without undercharging?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d need to count timber, fixings and hours from the drawing, then add delivery and waste. I’ve done that in my head for years, but I want to know where the contractor’s software hides the costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about if fewer sites opened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d worry about Leon, our newest apprentice, because he has less practice when a drawing misses a detail. You asked whether fewer office planners means fewer site starts; I don’t know that it does, since bookings here are already scarce. I’d show Leon the tool and handwork together, though I can’t promise the contractor will keep every role.

say: The office may send **cleaner drawings** and order materials sooner.
A good carpenter still has to make pieces meet when a **crooked building** makes the fit difficult.
think: Faster office planning does not tell me how many sites will open, and local **bookings are scarce**.
My hands-on work is harder to copy today, but I do not know how long that **advantage lasts**.
do: Learn the **contractor’s** estimating and drawing tools while leading carpentry work.
Ask the site manager to let me price **small jobs** during the first year.
Keep saving a portion of every **pay**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because local starts may shrink and my cushion is small.
S1.quote: My hands-on work is harder to copy today, but I do not know how long that advantage lasts.
fieldNote: Jamal sees a near-term change to office work, but does not assume faster planning will create or remove **site starts**.
He wants to help Leon learn, while admitting he cannot control the contractor’s **staffing choices**.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on active building sites
Learn the contractor’s estimating and drawing software for small job prices
Save a portion of each pay while site work remains available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the drawings and the office calls may change overnight, so we should keep a record of the hours and materials on each job. I would not tell them that my trade is safe, because the card says the robots follow in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, the planning and records part of my lead role could be done by AGI, and in 2031 the physical work could be done too. I might get some years of wages, but I can’t call carpentry protected or assume another contractor will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep taking site jobs and build a cash buffer while I still can. In 2029 I’d check the contractor’s workload and apply to other construction crews if mine had cut hours, even though their work could face the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not helpless; my skills and contacts can buy time, but not certainty. Two years is too short to build much savings from my current pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned applying to another crew, though you expect robots to reach hands-on work by 2031. How could that protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It may only give me a little time, and I don’t know if there will be an opening. I’d apply because losing hours before 2031 would hurt now, not because I think another crew is permanently safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours dropped in 2029, what would you and Nia decide about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d look at the lease and the cost of moving closer to her work before agreeing to a cheaper place farther out. We have no children or house plans to protect, but moving costs money we have not saved yet.

say: We should record each job’s **hours and materials** if the office tools change quickly.
I would not promise the crew that carpentry is **safe from robots**.
think: AGI could take my planning and records by **2028**, then robots could reach the physical work in 2031.
Another contractor might offer time, but no one can promise a **lasting opening**.
do: Build a **cash buffer** from site wages while I still have regular work.
Apply to other **construction crews** in **2029** if my hours are cut.
Review the **lease and moving costs** with Nia before choosing a cheaper flat.
feel: I feel **anxious but not helpless**; two years gives little time to save.
S2.quote: I might get some years of wages, but I can’t call carpentry protected or assume another contractor will hire me.
fieldNote: Jamal names the **thinking and hands-on sequence** without treating interim work as protection.
The proposed move depends on Nia’s job and costs they have not yet **put aside**.

steps.text: Build a cash buffer from each site wage before hours fall
Apply to other construction crews if the current contractor cuts hours in 2029
Compare lease and moving costs with Nia before choosing another flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives a crew a chance to learn new tools and get the paperwork in order. I would still tell the apprentices that the robot date is 2034, not that our site work lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The records and planning could leave my job in 2031, even if there is still a human crew on site for a while. Robots in 2034 make the hands-on part exposed too, so I have time to plan but no guaranteed next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the contractor to train me on its new planning system and keep leading the crew while there are jobs. In 2032, after thinking AGI arrives, I’d review my hours and pay with Nia and apply for site work if the contractor still has openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me less rushed than the 2028 picture, and I still expect a real threat to my income. I’d sleep better if our savings lasted longer than a few weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years let you do that the 2028 date did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save through several more pay cycles and learn the system on real jobs instead of trying to guess. It also gives me time to ask Leon and the other crew members what they are hearing, though nobody knows the hiring plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leon if the 2031 planning tools started reducing the crew’s hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Leon to keep a list of his hours and ask the foreman directly about next month’s roster. I wouldn’t tell him to switch into office planning as a safe answer, because that work is exposed too.

say: Five years gives crews time to learn **new tools** and sort out job records.
I would tell apprentices the **2034 robot date** is part of the picture.
think: Planning and records could leave my lead role in **2031**.
Robots expose the hands-on work later, so time helps without promising a **next job**.
do: Ask the contractor to train me on its new site **planning system**.
Keep leading the **carpentry** crew while building work remains available.
Review my **hours and pay** with Nia in **2032**, then apply if openings remain.
feel: I feel less rushed than in the 2028 picture, but still **anxious about income**.
S3.quote: I’d say five years gives a crew a chance to learn new tools and get the paperwork in order.
fieldNote: Jamal uses the longer lead time for **learning and saving**, not a claim of safety.
He explicitly rejects office planning as a fallback because it faces the same **thinking AI**.

steps.text: Learn the contractor’s new site planning system on active jobs
Keep leading the carpentry crew while the contractor has site work
Apply for available site work after reviewing pay and hours in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is enough time to make choices in stages, not enough time to ignore the change. The site crew should understand that the 2036 date reaches planning first and the 2039 date reaches the hands-on jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a decade of wages to build a cushion and learn the systems the contractor uses. I don’t think desk planning is a protected career after full AGI, and the later robots still put my carpentry work at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working, use AI for site paperwork and save steadily instead of waiting for a crisis. In 2037 I’d check whether the contractor still needs a human crew, and look for construction work elsewhere if my hours or pay had fallen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me room to act, which feels better than two. I’m still uneasy about whether my trade will provide income later, especially while our current cushion is so small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nia want to decide before the 2036 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d agree how much of our income should go to savings and whether we want to stay in this flat if my work changes. We have no child or wedding plans now, so I wouldn’t invent a deadline we haven’t chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend money on a longer course while you have ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take short, paid training the contractor offers before I borrow for a long course. I don’t know what jobs will remain after 2039, so debt for a promise would feel reckless.

say: Ten years lets us make choices in **stages**, but it is not a reason to ignore the change.
The **2036 date** reaches planning before robots reach hands-on site work.
think: I could use several years of wages to build a better **cash cushion**.
Desk planning is exposed after full AGI, and robots still threaten my **carpentry work**.
do: Keep working, use **AI** for site paperwork, and save steadily now.
Check the contractor’s crew needs in **2037** and apply elsewhere if pay or hours fall.
Choose **short paid training** rather than borrowing for a long course.
feel: Ten years feels more manageable, though I remain **uneasy about later income**.
S4.quote: I don’t think desk planning is a protected career after full AGI, and the later robots still put my carpentry work at risk.
fieldNote: Jamal treats the decade as **usable time**, not a guarantee that skills stay valuable.
He and Nia have no fixed family deadline, and avoid borrowing for **uncertain work**.

steps.text: Keep working on the current carpentry crew while jobs are available
Use AI for site paperwork and take contractor paid training
Save steadily from site pay into the shared emergency account
Apply to other construction crews if hours or pay fall after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years is hardly time to build savings before office work changes, and robots follow in 2031. A steadier run of paid site work and clear notice about the contractor’s staffing would help me plan with Nia.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how often a construction worker gets paid between projects, because a job title hides the gaps. I’m proud to lead a crew, but pride doesn’t pay rent when the site gate stays shut.

headlineQuote: I’m proud to lead a crew, but pride doesn’t pay rent when the site gate stays shut.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** crew lead with a trade certificate and a reputation for solving awkward carpentry problems.
He lives with his partner Nia and has **thin savings** despite earning lower pay for his job.
He uses new tools readily, but knows local construction jobs are **few** and may not be a safe fallback.
More warning gives him time to save and learn; it does not remove the risk to **planning and hands-on work**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries him most because it leaves little time before planning changes and robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A steady run of **paid site work** and clear notice about contractor staffing would help him plan with Nia.
